actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range:
This species is distributed throughout the entire tropical Indo-Pacific region. It is found from the Red Sea and East Africa in the west to the Hawaiian Islands (USA), Marquesas Islands (French Polynesia) and Ducie Atoll (Pitcairn Islands, UK) in the east. It is found in the north from southern Japan and south  to south eastern and western Australia including Lord Howe Island (Australia) and Rapa (G.R. Allen pers. comm. 2006). Vagrants are occasionally seen in the eastern Pacific at the Galapagos Islands (Ecuador). It has been recorded at depths of one to 61 m.
Range size ~82.2 million km2, from values estimated by Jones et al. (2002) based on projection of distribution maps from Allen et al. (1998).
documentation.population: This species is generally common (e.g., mean of 0.7 individuals per 20 0m2 in northern Great Barrier Reef; Pratchett and Berumen 2008). It has however, exhibited significant declines in abundance on the Great Barrier Reef (Pratchett 2001) and in French Polynesia (Berumen and Pratchett 2006) following extensive coral loss.
documentation.habitats: This species inhabits a wide variety of coral reef habitat, and can be encountered in coastal, lagoonal, and outer reefs (G.R. Allen pers. comm. 2006). It feeds mainly by tearing pieces from polychaetes, sea anemones, coral polyps, and algae (Myers 1991). It may be found singly, in pairs and in aggregations. This species only very rarely consumes coral on the Great Barrier Reef (Pratchett 2005), but consumes mainly live corals in the Indian Ocean (Graham et al. 2006). It declined significantly in Moorea between 1979 and 2003, following shifts in coral community structure (Berumen and Pratchett 2006).
documentation.threats: While declines in abundance of C. auriga have been observed following localized coral loss, it is unknown why this species should have any reliance on live corals. It neither feeds or recruits on live coral (Pratchett et al. 2008). This species is collected for the aquarium trade however there is no data on how this affects the population. This species is harvested by artisanal fishers, accounting for 72% of the butterflyfishes caught (Mangi and Roberts 2006).
documentation.measures: There are no species-specific conservation measures in place for Chaetodon auriga. This species is present within marine protected areas. Ongoing monitoring of  catches by aquarium collectors is required. Research is required to confirm or understand the apparent reliance on live corals for this species.
documentation.use_trade: Large volumes of this species (>25,000 individuals) are reported to have been exported for aquarium markets (GMAD 2009). It is a very common aquarium trade species.
documentation.rationale: There have been declines in the abundance of C. auriga in some areas and research is required to understand apparent reliance on live corals. It is collected for the aquarium trade but the impacts are unknown. Given that this species is very widespread and typically abundant, it is unlikely that localized declines have substantially affected the global population. It is listed as Least Concern.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: The Red Sea population generally lacks the dark spot on the soft dorsal fin. This population has been described as the sub-species C. auriga setifer Ahl 1923. However most recent authors regard it a conspecific with C. auriga.
